summary: LAN and WAN, intranet and Internet, client-server and peer-to-peer models, wired and wireless connections, and bus, ring, star and mesh topologies.

rows: Small: one building or site (school, office, home)
Large: cities, countries, the whole world
Uses infrastructure of telecom companies (leased lines, satellites)
Fibre-optic cables, telephone lines, satellite, microwave
The Internet; a bank linking all its branches

rows: Global public network of interconnected networks
Private network of one organisation using Internet technologies (web pages, browsers, TCP/IP)
Only authorised members (employees, students), often only inside the organisation
Public information from millions of sources
Internal information: timetables, policies, forms, news
Higher — behind a firewall, logins required
Controlled by the organisation, usually reliable

blocks.title: Extranet
blocks.content: Part of an intranet made available to **selected outsiders** (e.g. parents or suppliers) through a secure login.

items.title: Client-server
items.content: One or more powerful **servers** provide services (files, email, web, printing, logins); **clients** request them. Management, security and backup are **central**.

items.title: Peer-to-peer (P2P)
items.content: All computers are **equal**: each can share its own files and resources and use those of others. No central server.

rows: Central — accounts, permissions, antivirus managed on the server
Each user manages their own computer; weaker security
Slows down as more users share resources
Slower; varies with distance and obstacles
Interference from walls and other devices
Harder to intercept — physical access needed
Signals can be intercepted — needs encryption (WPA2/WPA3)
Users move freely; phones and tablets connect
Cables are costly to lay; trip hazard
Easy to add devices, no cables
Up to ~100 m per copper cable (fibre much more)
Limited by router range (~30–50 m indoors)

blocks.content: The **layout** of how the devices (nodes) of a network are connected.

blocks.title: Advantages and disadvantages
rows: **Bus** — all devices on one backbone cable with terminators
Cheap, little cable, easy to add a device
Backbone failure stops the whole network; collisions → slow with many devices; hard to find faults
**Ring** — each device connected to two others in a loop; data travels in one direction
No collisions; performs well under heavy load; order of access is fair
One broken link or device can stop the network; adding devices disrupts it
**Star** — every device connected to a central switch/hub
A failed cable affects only one device; easy to add devices; fast with a switch; easy to find faults
Central switch is a single point of failure; more cable; switch costs money
Very reliable — many routes; no single point of failure; can carry a lot of traffic
Expensive — lots of cables/links; complex to set up and manage

blocks.content: The Internet is a **mesh** of networks (many routes between routers). Most school and home LANs are **star** networks.
